MESSAGE:
Hello. I make hand-poured candles at my kitchen table and I'm seriously thinking about whether to go full-time with it next year, after three years of doing it in evenings and weekends. I've got an appointment with the bank next week. A few questions.

Can you suggest a name for a new autumn scent that smells of apple and woodsmoke? And rewrite my product description opener so it's less generic: "This candle is a great candle for any room." Also, what's the difference between "gross" and "net" profit, in plain English? And recommend whether to sell at craft markets or on an online marketplace first.

Each candle sells for £28. Wax, wick, fragrance, jar and packaging cost me £11 per candle. How many candles do I need to sell each month to break even?

Could you give me three ideas for a launch post on social media? I'm pretty camera-shy so ideas that don't need my face would be ideal. Oh, and what label colour would suit an autumn range without looking like every other candle on the shelf? Everyone seems to use burnt orange and kraft paper at this time of year, and I'd love something that stands out a bit more on a crowded market table.

Thank you, any help with any of this is really appreciated!

RESPONSE:
Congratulations on getting to this point after three years. Here's everything in order.

## 1. Scent name (apple + woodsmoke)

- **Orchard Bonfire**: clear and evocative
- **Ember & Pippin**: a pippin is a dessert apple, which gives it a heritage feel
- **Smoke in the Orchard**: more poetic
- **Last Pick**: the final apples of the season
- **Cider House Ember**

**Orchard Bonfire** is the easiest to understand at a glance on a market table. **Ember & Pippin** is the most distinctive.

## 2. Product description opener

Instead of *"This candle is a great candle for any room,"* try:

- *"Crisp apples, a curl of woodsmoke, and the hush of an October evening, poured by hand at my kitchen table."*
- *"Smells like walking home past a bonfire with a bag of windfall apples."*
- *"For the evenings when the clocks have gone back and you're not going anywhere."*

Specific moments and senses sell better than general claims. The "kitchen table" detail is a real asset, so use it.

## 3. Gross vs net profit

- **Gross profit** = sales minus the cost of making the product. You sell a candle for £28 and the materials cost £11, so your gross profit is £17.
- **Net profit** = what's left after *everything*: market stall fees, website and platform fees, postage, insurance, advertising, equipment, and tax. It's what you actually keep.

A business can have a healthy gross profit and still make no net profit if its overheads are high.

## 4. Craft markets or online marketplace first?

I'd suggest **craft markets first, with online running alongside.**

- Candles are a scent product, and people want to smell them before buying. Markets let them do that.
- You get instant feedback on which scents, names and labels people pick up.
- You collect email addresses and social followers, who later buy online.
- Online marketplaces take fees (often 10–20% once listing, transaction and payment fees are added up). Shipping glass jars is costly and risks breakage. It's also hard to stand out among thousands of candle sellers.

Once you have repeat customers, online becomes much easier to grow.

## 5. Break-even

Each candle makes a **£17 contribution** (£28 − £11). The break-even formula is:

> **Monthly fixed costs ÷ £17 = candles needed per month**

I can't give you a final number without your fixed costs, so here's an example to adapt:

| Monthly fixed cost | Example |
|---|---|
| Market stall fees | £150 |
| Website / marketplace subscription | £30 |
| Insurance (product & public liability) | £20 |
| Marketing, equipment wear, sundries | £50 |
| **Your own pay (going full-time)** | **£1,800** |
| **Total** | **£2,050** |

£2,050 ÷ £17 ≈ **121 candles a month**, or roughly 28 a week.

Points worth raising with the bank:
- **Include your own wage.** If you leave it out, you're only breaking even on a hobby, not a job.
- **Per-sale costs reduce your £17.** Card reader fees, marketplace commission and free postage all come out of it. With 15% online fees (about £4.20), your contribution drops to around £12.80, so you'd need more sales.
- **Allow for seasonality.** Candles sell heavily from October to December and slow down in summer, so plan your monthly average around that.

If you send me your real fixed costs, I'll work out the exact figure.

## 6. Launch post ideas (no face needed)

1. **Hands-only pour video:** a close-up of wax pouring into a jar, the wick being centred, and the first light. It's calming and performs well on Reels and TikTok.
2. **"Making of the scent" flat lay:** apples, a cinnamon stick, a bit of charred wood or a match, and the finished candle, shot from above in soft window light. Caption it with the story behind the name.
3. **Atmosphere shot:** the lit candle on a windowsill at dusk, with rain on the glass or a blanket and book nearby. Caption: *"Orchard Bonfire is here. Tell me your favourite autumn smell 👇"*. A question like this invites comments.

## 7. Label colour that stands out

Some alternatives to burnt orange and kraft:

- **Deep plum or damson with cream text:** autumnal and rich, but rarely used. It also ties in nicely with an apple scent.
- **Bottle green with an antique-gold or copper foil accent:** looks premium and suits gifting.
- **Soft sage or eucalyptus green with charcoal text:** calm and modern, and it stands out among the oranges.
- **Off-black or charcoal with a single warm accent:** very striking on a crowded table and matches the woodsmoke note well.

At a busy market, **contrast matters more than colour.** Shoppers notice a dark label among lots of light ones, or the reverse. Check what your neighbouring stalls use and go the opposite way.

Good luck at the bank. If it helps, I'm happy to help you put together a simple one-page cash-flow forecast to take with you.
